title: Hadjod (Cissus quadrangularis): Benefits, Uses and Safety
excerpt: Hadjod (Cissus quadrangularis) is the Ayurvedic bone setter plant. What the studies show on fractures and joints, its side effects, and how to grow it.
content:
Quick answer: Hadjod (Cissus quadrangularis), also called bone setter or devil's backbone, is a fleshy, four-angled climbing vine from the grape family that Ayurveda has long used for broken bones and joint pain. Lab and animal studies are encouraging, but the human evidence is thin: a 2017 review of 9 clinical studies (1,108 participants) rated the fracture evidence as low quality, and a 2025 review rated its effect on bone markers as very low certainty. It does not replace a cast, a surgeon, or your prescribed medicines.

Walk through almost any village in Odisha, Tamil Nadu or Maharashtra and you will probably spot hadjod scrambling over a fence or a neem tree, its green stems looking like a string of sausages joined end to end. Many Indian families keep a cutting at home because a grandparent swore by it after a fall. In the US and UK the same plant turns up as a capsule on supplement shelves, sold for joints, bones and weight loss.

What is the Hadjod plant?

Hadjod is a perennial succulent climber in the Vitaceae, the same family as the grapevine. Its accepted botanical name is Cissus quadrangularis L., first published by Linnaeus in 1767. "Quadrangularis" means four-angled, which describes the stem.

According to Kew's Plants of the World Online, the plant is native to tropical and southern Africa, Madagascar, the Arabian Peninsula and the Indian subcontinent through to Myanmar, and it grows mainly in the seasonally dry tropics. India Flora Online, run by the herbarium at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru, records it in dry deciduous and thorn forests, scrub jungle and wasteland across states including Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Maharashtra.

It goes by many names. India Flora Online lists these:

LanguageNames
EnglishBone setter, adamant creeper, edible-stemmed vine
HindiHarjora, Harsenkari (commonly written Hadjod)
OdiaHadasara, Hodabhanga, Harsingaari, Hadasinkuda
TamilPirandai, Pirandi
MalayalamChanamparanda, Changalamparanda, Peranta

In Ayurvedic texts it appears as Asthisamharaka or Asthishrunkhala. "Asthi" means bone, and "shrunkhala" means chain, a fair description of how the stem segments link together.

How do you identify Hadjod?

The stem gives it away. It is thick, fleshy and square in cross-section, with a narrow wing along each of the four corners, and it is pinched into segments a few inches long. Older segments can turn reddish or brown. Look for these features:

  • Thin, coiled tendrils that grab any nearby support.
  • Small, simple leaves, often three-lobed or heart-shaped, set alternately on the stem. They drop easily, so a mature plant can look almost leafless.
  • Tiny greenish-yellow flowers in small clusters.
  • Pea-sized berries that turn red and then dark when ripe.

What is Hadjod used for in Ayurveda?

In Hindi, "had" means bone and "jod" means joint or join, so hadjod is literally "bone joiner." In Ayurvedic practice the stem is crushed for juice, dried into powder, or made into a paste and applied over an injury. Practitioners use it mainly for fractures and joint pain. A 2021 review in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology, written by researchers in Maharashtra, also lists traditional uses for piles, gout, colic, skin diseases, fever and digestive complaints.

Ayurvedic doctors often recommend taking the juice with ghee or warm milk after a fracture. These tips come from tradition. No trial has tested them as a regimen.

In South Indian kitchens the plant is also a food. In Tamil Nadu, the young stems are cleaned, fried with urad dal and spices, and ground into pirandai thuvaiyal, a thick chutney. North Indian home cooks make a similar chutney with moong dal and coconut. Cooks usually peel the stems wearing gloves or with oiled hands, because handling the raw stem can make your skin itch.

Does Hadjod actually help broken bones heal?

It might help a little, but the evidence is weak.

The best summary so far is a 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis in Phytotherapy Research by Sawangjit and colleagues. They searched 12 databases and found 9 randomized trials with 1,108 participants in total, covering several different conditions. Cissus had a significant effect on bone pain, and the authors concluded it had a benefit for fractures. They also rated the fracture evidence as low quality under the GRADE system and said better studies were still needed. In plain terms, the fracture trials were small or flawed enough that the real effect could turn out much smaller, or nothing at all.

A 2025 review in BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies from Chiang Mai University looked at blood markers of bone health. Across 7 trials with 354 people, Cissus raised parathyroid hormone levels but did not change calcium, phosphorus or alkaline phosphatase. The certainty of evidence was very low for all four markers, and most of the trials had some risk of bias.

Animal and test-tube studies look more promising. A 2013 review by Stohs and Ray concluded they support Cissus for fracture healing and as an anti-osteoporosis agent, but rats are not people. A broken bone still needs an X-ray, proper alignment and immobilization, and the herb has not been shown to speed any of that up in reliable human trials.

What other benefits have been studied?

Researchers have tested hadjod extracts for a long list of effects. The 2021 Journal of Ethnopharmacology review describes lab and animal work showing pain-relieving, anti-inflammatory, anticonvulsant, antimicrobial, anticancer and anti-osteoporosis activity. None of this shows the same effect in people.

Weight loss is the other big claim, and the one behind most Western supplement sales. The 2017 meta-analysis found that Cissus combination products beat placebo for body weight, cholesterol, triglycerides and fasting blood sugar, with an average extra weight loss of about 5.2 kg. Those products mixed Cissus with other ingredients, though. In a 10-week trial in Cameroon published in 2008, for example, the strongest results came from Cissus combined with African mango seed (Irvingia gabonensis), which makes it hard to credit Cissus alone. The same review found no benefit for hemorrhoids, even though piles are a classic traditional use.

Chemists have found flavonoids, triterpenoids, alkaloids, saponins, iridoids, stilbenes, steroids and glycosides in the plant. A 2025 review in Frontiers in Plant Science from VIT Vellore highlights its ketosteroids and flavonoids as the compounds most likely behind its bone effects. It also notes that the plant uses a water-saving form of photosynthesis, which helps explain how it survives long dry spells.

Is Hadjod safe to take?

Short courses of tested extracts look fairly safe. The Stohs and Ray review called the extracts safe at commonly used doses, and the 2017 meta-analysis found no serious side effects across its trials. In the 2008 Cameroon trial, the side effects reported most often were headache, trouble sleeping and gas, but the placebo group had them too.

That reassurance has limits:

  • No agreed dose. There is no established safe dose for fresh stem, juice or powder. Products and home preparations vary widely, so take it only with guidance from a qualified doctor or registered Ayurvedic practitioner.
  • Pregnancy and breastfeeding. There is no reliable safety data for pregnant or breastfeeding women. The 2008 Cameroon trial, for example, excluded them. Avoid it unless your doctor approves.
  • Diabetes medicines. Several Cissus products lowered fasting blood sugar in trials. If you take insulin or tablets for diabetes, talk to your doctor first so your sugar does not drop too low.
  • Raw stem. Do not chew raw stems on your own. Traditional recipes always clean and cook them.
  • Long-term use. Most trials lasted a few weeks to a few months, so long-term safety has not been studied.

Hadjod also does not replace calcium, vitamin D or any medicine your doctor has prescribed for osteoporosis or arthritis. If you think you have broken a bone, get it examined and immobilized first.

How do you grow Hadjod at home?

Hadjod is one of the easier medicinal plants to grow, especially in warm parts of India. In the wild it grows in dry scrub, so treat it more like a cactus than a fern:

  • Soil: Well-drained sandy or loamy mix. A cactus and succulent mix works in pots.
  • Light: Full sun to partial shade. A sunny balcony or terrace is ideal.
  • Water: Moderate. Let the soil dry out between waterings, because soggy roots rot faster than drought hurts it.
  • Warmth: It likes heat. In the UK and northern US, bring it indoors before the first frost.
  • Propagation: Take a stem cutting of two or three segments, let it dry for a day, then push one joint into moist soil.
  • Support: Give it a trellis, railing or stake, and the tendrils will do the rest.

Even if you never use it as medicine, it makes an unusual ornamental, and insects visit its small flowers.

So, should you use Hadjod?

If you enjoy pirandai chutney, cooked hadjod has been part of Indian diets for generations. As a medicine, treat it as a possible extra, not a fix. The human trials so far are small, and their quality is low to very low. If you want to try a capsule or powder for joint pain or after an injury, tell your doctor, follow the product's labeled directions, and keep your regular treatment going.

Health disclaimer: This article is for general information only and is not medical advice. Hadjod is not a proven treatment for fractures, osteoporosis or any other condition. Talk to a qualified doctor before using it, especially if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, have diabetes, or take any regular medicines. Research details are accurate as of November 2026.

FAQ

What is Hadjod called in English and Odia?

In English it is usually called bone setter, devil's backbone, veldt grape or adamant creeper. India Flora Online lists the Odia names as Hadasara, Hodabhanga, Harsingaari and Hadasinkuda. In Tamil it is pirandai.

Can Hadjod heal a fracture on its own?

No. A fracture needs a medical exam, an X-ray and proper immobilization. As of November 2026, the human evidence that Hadjod helps bones heal is rated low quality. Treat it as a possible supplement alongside medical care, never instead of it.

How much Hadjod should I take a day?

There is no established safe dose for fresh stem, juice or homemade powder. Commercial capsules list their own directions, but those are set by the manufacturer, not by health authorities. Ask a qualified doctor or Ayurvedic practitioner before you start.

Does Hadjod help with weight loss?

Some trials found weight and cholesterol benefits, but mostly from products that combined Cissus with other ingredients. There is no strong evidence that Hadjod by itself causes meaningful weight loss.

Can I eat Hadjod stems?

Yes, cooked. In South India the young stems are peeled and cooked into chutneys and other dishes. Avoid eating the raw stem without guidance, and wear gloves when you peel it, since it can irritate the skin.

Is Hadjod safe during pregnancy?

Its safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and clinical trials such as the 2008 Cameroon study left pregnant and breastfeeding women out. Avoid it unless your doctor specifically approves.
